segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, how the quality of your diet is probably more important than obsessing on the individual parts of it.
Drugs and palliative care which make distress worse and can even kill you. An investment strategy for the government which could tap into potential earnings of around $60 billion.
Not bad money when the bean counters are looking for every cent. And how optimism might save your life.
A 70,000 person study has linked optimism to around a 30% reduction in the risk of premature death from any cause.
The lead author is Eric Kim of Harvard School of Public Health in Boston.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Thank you.
What did we know about optimism and its relation to life expectancy, dying prematurely before you did your study?
There's been studies linking optimism with reduced risk of death from coronary heart disease, cardiovascular outcomes.
However, there's never been a study looking at different causes of outcomes as well.
Now, I should have explained this at the beginning, but I mean, we kind of think we know what optimism is, but maybe you should actually just explain it.
In a nutshell, it's the expectation that things will be better than worse.
And what's really interesting is that people think that optimistic people are just always chipper and sunny people.
However, what's also interesting is that people might not necessarily present that way, but also have just the internal belief that things will get better.
So they're not necessarily happy chappies.
Yes, but do believe things will get better.
So your study looked, this is a nurse's study, which we've had on the health report many times over the years.
It's an extraordinarily large study, tens of thousands of women followed over decades.
And you've obviously done a psychological profile on these women and seen what happens to them.
There's a well-validated optimism measure and ask questions like,
in uncertain times, I usually expect the best or I hardly ever expect things to go my way.
And there's a series of questions like this, and you can assess someone's level of optimism.
And then we looked and tracked people's survival over time, as well as lots of other factors.
And what did you find?
We found that when we looked at people with the highest optimism versus lowest optimism,
so top 25 versus bottom 25, the most optimistic had about a 29% reduced risk of mortality.
And we also controlled for all kinds of different confounders and saw that the association kept
persisting.
When you say reduced risk of mortality, mortality is 100%.
So you're talking about reduced mortality at your particular age.
Yes.
Now we're going to dissect optimism because some people who are pessimistic are depressed.
Yeah.
I also want to say something that I'm very passionate about and have seen a little bit
of, this idea of potential victim blaming.
People can have low optimism for all variety of reasons, some that are within our control,
but also a lot of factors that are not within our control, such as parental warmth when
someone's younger actually predicts someone's optimism.
Levels of education and wealth is a weak, but it is a predictor of optimism as well.
So I'm assuming with parental warmth, you're talking about the
emotionally in-tune parent who sets limits, but within a loving environment.
Yes, something like that.
And how much of it is genetic or really pre-programmed into your personality?
There's been some twin studies and it shows that about 25% of it is heritable,
which suggests that there is things that we can do to influence our levels of optimism.

So you've adjusted for all these things, your diet, whether you're depressed, and you still find that optimism by itself seems to reduce your risk, particularly of heart disease and cancer and other causes of premature death.
Yes.
So what is it about optimism that does it?
There are three potential pathways.
And one is that optimism may influence better health.
For example, past studies have shown that optimistic people actually eat healthier, exercise more and acquire better sleep.
And a second pathway might be that optimists have better coping skills.
And there is a recent review of over 50 studies.
And they show that optimists in general use better coping methods.
Like they seek support more when in stressful times they plan for challenges and they have more contingency plans.
Like if plan A doesn't go well, then they plan for B and C.
And the third potential pathway is that optimism may actually directly influence our biology.
Now, it's that last one we've looked at a couple of times on the health report, particularly looking at people who've already got cancer.
And this comes to your caveat a few moments ago,
which is that you can blame the person for not being optimistic.
So they looked at people with cancer in Australia
and then tracked them through according to their attitude
and their middle attitude, are they optimistic or pessimistic?
And it made absolutely no difference to the outcome once you had cancer
because one of the problems is that if your cancer comes back,
people say, oh, well, you didn't have a positive enough attitude.
I'm not aware of that particular study,
but these were healthier people at baseline
and we weren't looking at people who had serious illnesses.
So that might be a different subset.
So when you find this sort of association in a study like this,
it's not necessarily cause and effect.
You try and find out whether it is,
but really all you can say is the link is strong between optimism
and a 30% reduced risk of dying prematurely from all-cause mortality.
So that's fine, but it's not cause and effect yet.
To prove it's cause and effect,
you change somebody from a pessimistic attitude towards life
to an optimistic view.
Is there any evidence at all that changing one's view of the world and life changes your mortality rate?
I think there were three studies published in JAMA Internal Medicine, and I'll tell you an example of one of them.
There were people who had a heart condition, they had a heart procedure, and over the period of a year, they induced positive emotions in one group and the other half had standard of care.
And in the group where they induced positive emotions, they were actually 1.7 times more likely to achieve their physician-recommended levels of physical activity.
And the other studies actually showed higher medication adherence and things like that.
So there are some really promising and interesting randomized control studies where we can pinpoint causality,
showing that when we induce these positive mental states, that it could change our health behaviors.
And are there reliable techniques for switching you to the optimism mode?
There are some easier ones that have smaller effect sizes and then more time and resource intensive ones that have larger effect sizes and are more reliable.
and I'll start with the easier ones first. One is just listing things that you're grateful for
every day. And a randomized study showed that if you do it for seven days, then your optimism will
increase a little bit. Another showed that if you list things that you do that are kind over a period
of 14 days, that can also increase your optimism a bit. Where you've been kind to somebody else.
Yes, listing your instances of kindness throughout the day. And then a third one is called best
possible self. And you think about your different domains of life, whether it be maybe one domain is
your relationship with your partner or spouse, another one's your career, another one's your
friendships. And you think about the best possible outcome. And then the next six days, you vividly
try to imagine that. And that's also been shown to increase optimism a bit. Some of the more
resource and time intensive ones include mindfulness meditation, different forms of
cognitive behavioral therapy, and something called hope therapy. So those require a bit more work,
but they do have a larger effect. Yes. Eric Kim, thank you very much for joining us on The Health
Report. Thank you so much. Eric Kim is at Harvard School of Public Health in Boston. And in a related
story, be sure to listen to the next episode of All in the Mind, when Lynn Malcolm explores the
field of social genomics, how adverse life circumstances such as deep loneliness can
increase the gene activity that leads to chronic disease, and how having a sense of meaning in life
can be protective against disease. That's on Sunday afternoon at five o'clock and online
on Radio National. Meantime, you're with The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and
CBC radio across Canada. Let's stay with keeping your mortal coil as healthy as possible for as
long as possible and move from your mind to your diet. Australian research has found that focusing
on your whole diet rather than obsessing on individual nutrients pays off in terms of obesity
and blood pressure and that our official dietary guidelines do seem to work which no doubt has a
lot of experts breathing a sigh of relief. The bad news is that you still have to stay off junk food.
Catherine Livingston of Deakin University did a lot of the work on this study
and she's in our Melbourne studio.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Thank you.
Why choose obesity and blood pressure?
So obesity and hypertension are really major health problems
facing the average Australian population.
We know, for example, two in every three adults are overweight or obese
and one in every three adults have hypertension.
And it's really potentially quite interesting,
the relationship between risk of obesity and hypertension
and the combined effects.
So up to 75% of hypertension
is thought to be caused by being overweight or obese.
So if we're able to understand
how we can tackle these major health issues,
we can really make a meaningful impact
on the overall health of the population.
And of course, one of the ways we can do this,
as you said, is through diet.
So you looked at the extent to which people...
Tell us about the study that you did.
So in this study, we were looking at individuals
following the Australian dietary guidelines.

As many of your listeners will know, the Australian Dietary Guidelines provide really useful key information on the types and the amounts of the foods that we should eat to promote health and well-being.
And I think what's really important to distinguish in these recommendations is that we have things that we should eat more of in our diet.
So these are the beautiful fruits and the vegetables and the whole grains and things that we should limit.
So things that are high in saturated fat and salt.
So these would be our crisps and our biscuits.
And so these are fantastic, clear messages to the public.
But what's really missing is evaluating how these updated recommendations that were issued in 2013 actually relate to these major health problems of obesity and high blood pressure.
So what did you find?
So in our study, we included just under 5,000 men and women.
And important to note that these were individuals from all across Australia.
So all states and territories, really great, fantastic nationally representative data.
and we derived two overall dietary scores.
And these were both based on the Australian Dietary Guidelines,
but there's quite an important difference in these two scores.
So the first one is based on whether individuals meet the recommendations
for what they should eat more of.
So these are the fruits and the vegetables,
but also what they should eat less of.
So these are high-fat cakes and crisps, for example.
Whereas the second score, we actually looked at what would happen
if individuals just met the recommended foods.
So if they just ate two portions of fruit, five of vegetables, they matched their intakes of whole grain, of lean meats and low-fat dairy.
And actually what we saw was really important differentiation between these two scores in that individuals were only associated with lower risk of obesity
if they had both recommended intakes of the things that they should eat more of and the things that they should eat less of.
So this is an important message to the public.
So it wasn't just that you could feel honourable by having your two fruits and five veg or five,
I don't know which way around it is, but that sort of thing and not much red meat and low fat and so on,
and low saturated fat.
You had to stay off the rubbish.
That's right.
So people really have to consider, yes, we've had great amounts of fruit and vegetables,
but that doesn't mean that there's an excuse then to go out and eat a whole block of chocolate.
We've got to keep that message of moderation in mind.
So where does the dietary pattern fit into this?
Because people obsess.
I was doing something which we recorded for the health report
at the Sydney Writers Festival recently,
and I've got 700 people or something in the audience
going to put up their hands.
How many are on a gluten-free diet?
80% put up their hands.
How many are on low carbs?
50% put up their hands.
I mean, people are obsessing on individual nutrients
rather than the whole diet.
I mean, presumably they're running the risk
of not being on the right diet.
That's right.
And there are a lot of what we call fad diets or celebrity endorsed diets out there.
And I think the key message coming from this study is that simply by following these tried and tested,
scientifically robust recommendations that we're going to achieve a really great impact on maintaining our weight
and maintaining healthy blood pressure.
So we shouldn't be fixated, as you said, on these single foods and these single nutrients.
And that's what the focus of the revised 2013 Australian Dietary Guidelines was,
much more food-based, overall diet-based.
Because as you said, we don't just eat a potato,
we're going to eat that as part of a whole meal.
We're going to have maybe our vegetables and maybe our meat.
And it's the impact of all of that together that's important.
And is there a translation to life expectancy here?
So we didn't look at life expectancy, particularly in this study,
but you would hope that with lower risk of obesity and hypertension
that that's going to have knock-on effects on their life expectancy.
But we didn't look at that specifically.
And do we all have to then go to the National Health and Medical Research Council's website
to find out the dietary guidelines and go cross-eyed?
Or is there a simple way of doing this?
I mean, you're saying it's the Mediterranean diet,
not a lot of red meat, white meat, monosaturated fats, etc.
That sort of dietary pattern.
Is that what it all boils down to?
Yeah, so the recommendations are up on the website, as you said,
but the key messages to the public is really you want to have a wide variety of foods,
So great colours and different components in there.
You want to have plenty of vegetables, plenty of fruits, plenty of whole grain foods.
So, for example, maybe once a week you might, instead of having the white rice, you'll have the whole grain rice.
Plenty of lean meats and eggs and legumes, low-fat dairy products and plenty of water.
So we're all tempted to maybe have the fizzy drink now and then just maybe to swap that for water more often.
And don't feel honourable and have a blowout.
Exactly. Everything in moderation and balance.
Catherine, look, thanks very much for joining us on The Health Report.
Thank you, it's a pleasure.
Catherine Livingston is in the Institute for Physical Activity and Nutrition at Deakin University.
People who are receiving palliative care are understandably often really distressed,
and that can manifest as confusion, disturbed communication,
and even the feeling that you're hallucinating.
That often gets doctors reaching for drugs called antipsychotics,
normally reserved for people with schizophrenia.
But these have been poorly researched in palliative care.
A recent Australian study, though, suggests that these medications may make distress worse and even reduce survival.
Meera Agar was the lead author.
Meera is a palliative medicine physician at the Centre for Cardiovascular and Chronic Care at the University of Technology, Sydney.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Thank you.
So just tell me the typical story here, the typical patient that you're talking about.
So we're talking about people with advanced illness where we know there's no longer a cure for their underlying illness
and that their life expectancy is shortened.
And we know that at least one in three of those people
will have a delirium episode at some point in their final months of life.
So delirium being what I just described,
and maybe you should just describe it in a bit more detail
because it's often missed by nursing and medical staff.
So delirium is a condition of the brain which is actually a medical emergency.
There are many medical issues that cause delirium,
including infection, changes in medication, changes in your body, metabolic states such
as liver or kidney failure.
And what happens is a whole raft of symptoms, confusion, agitation, hallucinations are often
the most noticeable ones.
But people's inability to focus attention, inability to communicate, drowsiness also
are part of the spectrum of delirium.
And often those are the ones that get missed.

So what you're saying is there are some symptoms, some people can be acting out and seeing things and really being very distressed and outward and hard to control in some ways, and other people can go very quiet.

And sometimes it's just assumed that because these people have an advanced illness that it's okay to have a day where you're a bit quiet and a bit down, and people often don't think that it might be delirium that's causing those sudden changes.
And when you say it's a medical emergency, why is it a medical emergency?
Because we need to actually try and assess what the underlying medical condition is very quickly
and get on top of those issues.
So if someone has an infection causing their delirium,
we need to be trying to treat that quickly and expediently
because the longer it has effects on the brain,
the poorer the outcomes for the delirium will be.
So tell us about the use of these antipsychotics
and why you were worried enough to do this study?
Because people raise the sign of the cross to these antipsychotics
in aged care and people with dementia.
I mean, you're talking about a very different group of people here,
but they're poisonous in aged care.
So we were, I suppose, interested in this area
because we, as clinicians, see the distress that delirium causes
for our patients and their families and others, the treating clinicians.
But we were looking at the evidence,

And though antipsychotics have been trialled in this situation, they haven't been compared to what we also are doing at that time, which is treating all these underlying causes, trying to explain to people what delirium is.
But a lot of other supportive measures that we can do to help people remain oriented to the environment.
and we wanted to see whether adding an antipsychotic
on top of doing all of those other things that we should be doing
added any extra value to just doing those things that we know are effective.
So in other words, this was a comparison against best palliative care.
Yes, correct.
And of course, there's a misconception about palliative care in the community.
They think it's just about doling out narcotics to make people's pain better,
but really it's about comprehensive symptom management.
And we know in hospitals, simple things, seemingly simple things
like having people have their glasses on, their hearing aids with batteries,
helping them have a glass of water, helping them walk around the ward.
These are things that often get missed in the busy hospital environments that we work in.
So you did a randomised trial and there were two drugs, haloperidol and risperidone.
What did you find?
So we found that after 72 hours of treatment where we allowed people to increase the dose
if distress continued, that the people in the risperidone and haloperidol arms had worse
symptoms than the people in the placebo arm.
Worse symptoms.
To what extent?
So it was a small extent, but we were actually wanting to see a benefit.
So it was in completely the opposite direction to if the drugs were actually helping reduce
distress.
And you found that haloperidol actually shortened survival?
So we found in the antipsychotic arms the survival was 1.5%.
The people in the antipsychotic arms had a 1.5 times reduced survival than the people in the placebo arm.
So a 50% increase in the risk of death.
What was causing that?
We're not sure.
These were people that were only receiving six doses over a 72-hour period.
It's possible because of the delirium not being relieved that that may have led to worsened mortality.
But we don't know whether they had longer term exposure to these drugs after the study period.
Now another drug that's headed out like Smarties in this sort of situation is olanzapine.
Why didn't you study olanzapine?
I suppose this was a very difficult trial to do.
And I think we had to pick medications which are commonly used in this situation.
But olanzapine is very commonly used.
And we also needed a matching placebo that could be matched to both the active agents
and both risperidone and haloperidol come in an oral solution.
And haloperidol is the most commonly used medication for delirium.
And what would you expect olanzapine to show in this sort of situation?
We would expect that it's quite a similar effect.
These are medications in a class and the fact that we found both haloperidol and risperidone
showed these difficulties, we would expect that other antipsychotics may also show problems with symptom control.
And is there any indication of brain damage?
In other words, that by giving these drugs you're actually changing things in the longer term
or it was very immediate, the effect?
So we started to see a difference in the symptom relief even at day one.
how that's modulated at a neurotransmitter level is not well understood. Delirium is a
condition where the basic science of what actually causes delirium is quite poorly understood.
So the key here is for family and friends to notice delirium, it's a change in cognitive state
and if that happens to quiet or to active they've got to draw people's attention to it
but the solution is not drugs. Yeah we need to be speaking to our patients and families and taking
changes in cognition or behaviour really seriously and respecting that if they have noticed a change
then that we need to pay attention and listen and respond quite quickly.
Meera, thanks for joining us.
Thank you.
Professor Meera Agar is a palliative medicine physician at the Centre for Cardiovascular and
Chronic Care at the University of Technology, Sydney.
According to the National Mental Health Commission, that's a national body that's supposed to
keep governments honest when it comes to mental health care in Australia,
Poor mental health costs the nation around $60 billion a year, an astounding figure.
The Commission also argues that there are investments that could recoup some of that waste.
To that end, they've brought out to Australia an expert in such economic data.
He's Professor Martin Knapp of the London School of Economics and Political Science, LSE.
Martin is in our Melbourne studio.
Welcome to Australia.
Thank you very much.
So $60 billion is a lot of money.
Yes, it's a lot of money, and I think some of it is very well spent
and some of it's probably not so appropriately spent.
I think part of the difficulty with mental health issues
is that quite often the way that we respond to them is through crises.
We have to respond to crises,
and some of those costs would also be outside the health sector
for things that perhaps we could have avoided,
like contact with criminal justice or unemployment and so on.
So I think there's a mix of what I would call good costs and bad costs in there.
Now, there's a two-way relationship between mental health problems and the economy.
I mean, poor economic circumstances can cause.
I mean, just take us through the two-way relationship.
Okay. Well, I mean, certainly it is the case that people who are in very difficult circumstances,
in poverty, who are facing long periods of unemployment, who have unmanageable debt,
are at greater risk getting mental health problems and those problems staying around for a long time.
But it's also the case that people who have those mental health problems will then have difficulties in getting a job or earning a decent income, forming relationships and so on.
So this is kind of a two-way street and it can for many people be a vicious cycle.
They lose their job.
They become stressed.
That makes it harder for them to get a job and things just get worse and worse.
now the bean counters in canberra are used to lobbying organizations coming up with
economic reports you know arthritis mental health cancer blah blah blah and they say oh it's just
another excess economics report and you know put it to one side because they all say it costs a
fortune and if only you'd spend money on it life would be a bit would be better and you'd save a
fortune um which is just the trap i fell into in my introduction i mean how much of this is bull
and how much is real?
A lot of this is real.
I mean, certainly the costs are real.
I think what we're trying to emphasise
in the discussions I've been having,
I've been here for a week now,
managed to pick up an Australian cold at the time,
but in the period I've been here,
it's emphasising that, you know,
there are ways in which these mental health problems
can be responded to or they can be prevented.
And there are very strong,
there's very strong evidence from lots of places,
including from the UK,
that that makes a lot of economic sense.

So we are trying to emphasize that it's not just a big number, but it's a number that can be brought down if we can do something, particularly if it's early in life or early in the course of the illness, to prevent it or to respond very quickly.
So let's look at some of these economic studies that you and others have done in the UK.
One is what can happen in the things that you can do in the emergency department.
Yes, I mean, one of the things that we're very concerned with in the UK,
I'm sure it's the same here,
is that many people who present at the emergency department,
perhaps after some self-harming,
they might get patched up by the emergency department,
but they don't get the psychosocial support they really need.
And what we've, not a study we've done,
but we've found other people's studies that have shown
that if you can provide a bit of psychosocial support
within the emergency department...
What does that mean, actually?
Well, it's actually firstly just recognising there might be something behind that injury which is reflecting a cry for help.
Somebody really is feeling very stressed. It might be in a suicide attempt. It might just be a cry for help.
Can you get that person into contact with services?
Maybe you can actually direct them into the services within the hospital setting depending on how severe their problem is.
But when you do that, the evidence shows it's very positive in terms of preventing further such episodes for that individual.
And that also makes economic sense too.
So a fairly brief intervention capturing it.
Yes, I think it's just recognised.
I mean, the emergency departments in the UK at least, they're incredibly stressful environments.
They're very, very busy.
You can understand the difficulties for staff.
But if you can just find a way, it may need a little bit of investment of a specialist in that setting,
a way of actually identifying these people and responding to their very desperate needs sometimes,
that can make a lot of sense.
And maternal mental health, mother's mental health?
Well, maternal mental health, I think, is a global issue in that probably half the cases of maternal mental health problems
during pregnancy in the early months after the birth don't get recognized and therefore don't get treated.
That's very bad for the mother, of course, but it's particularly bad for the child
because maternal mental health problems, postnatal depression is the most common,
that don't get treated can lead to the child having emotional difficulties,
behavioural problems, lower intelligence.
And so what we've done in one of our studies is shown how those consequences
through the child are very expensive.
Now, we did a study two years ago which just counted up those costs,
but I think it was sufficiently shocking to the UK government
that they then invested a lot of extra money in maternal mental health services.
And what we've done subsequently is then shown our National Health Service in England
what they can do in terms of better services for those mothers.
And does that make a difference?
Well, the services, there are interventions around that have been worked on.
They can be quite low level, just helping community professionals to identify problems and respond to them.
There might be a more heavy duty where a mother has a psychosis and they need much more concentrated support.
They do seem to work in terms of improving the mother's mental health and that will improve the mother's attachment and engagement with the child and that should improve the child's development.
And briefly, you've also looked at bullying.
Yeah, well, bullying, I think, is one of these problems, again, across the world.
We've shown that bullying in teenage years can lead to mental health problems and mental health costs even 40 years later.
So people at 50 who were bullied at age 7 show differences in their mental health and their use of services compared to those who weren't bullied at age 7.
So I think we can do something about that.
We would head off a lot of problems and costs.
Now, those are just three areas.
I want to go a few seconds left.
Those are just three areas.
I mean, there's a lot of emphasis in Australia in, say, early intervention in psychosis that might lead to schizophrenia.
I mean, are there enough studies around to make these, you know, to look at the whole area of mental health and interventions to really make the case for treasuries?
Well, I think there's a number of areas where we have got good evidence.
There's still loads more research is needed.
But I think we can, I can point to evidence across the lifespan.
And it's also interventions not just in the health sector.
It's things that can be done in schools, in workplaces, in communities to actually avoid, to prevent some of these problems occurring or responding very speedily when they do emerge.
Martin Knapp, who's Professor of Social Policy and Director of the Personal Social Services Research Unit at the London School of Economics and Political Science.
I'm Norman Swan. This has been The Health Report. I look forward to your company next week.
